entities.name: Theater an der Wien
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Theater an der Wien in Vienna, Austria, built in 1801 by Emanuel Schikaneder (librettist of Mozart's The Magic Flute), is one of the most historically significant opera and theatre venues in the world, famous as the site of world premieres of Beethoven's Fidelio (1805, 1806), his symphonies Nos. 2-8, and works by Mozart, Brahms, and Johann Strauss. The building where Beethoven himself lived while composing is a pilgrimage site for classical music history.

Emanuel Schikaneder, who had written the libretto and played Papageno in The Magic Flute premiere at Vienna's Freihaus-Theater (1791), built the Theater an der Wien to capitalize on his success. Beethoven lived in apartments in the building between 1803-1804 while composing Fidelio, and the theatre served as the primary venue for premieres of his orchestral and operatic works. The venue was crucial during the Congress of Vienna (1814-1815), when European heads of state attended performances nightly.

The theater was converted to a television studio in 1955, but restored to full opera house operation in 2001, becoming Vienna's second opera house (alongside the Staatsoper) with a focus on Baroque and Classical opera performance. Its programming under artistic director Roland Geyer earned it the 'Opera House of the Year' award multiple times. The intimate 1,000-seat auditorium enables a proximity to performance impossible at the Staatsoper's 1,700-seat scale.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Theater an der Wien, where Beethoven lived while composing and premiered his most important orchestral works, holds more classical music history within its walls than virtually any other building — making it a living archive of the Classical era's greatest achievements.
